1.e4 c5 2.Nc3.name: Closed Sicilian
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3.background: White's second most common move against 1...c5, after 2.Nf3. Many lines transpose into the Open Sicilian, the Moscow Variation or the Rossolimo Variation, and Andrew Soltis dubbed the set-up with 3.Nge2 the Chameleon System. The former world champion Boris Spassky often used the Closed Sicilian with success, even in Candidates matches.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and fights for d4 and e5 without committing a pawn. Black can wait to see which set-up White chooses, and if White drifts into an Open Sicilian, Black reaches a favourable version of it. Against a slow White set-up the game becomes a manoeuvring fight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Guards e5 and the c5-pawn and frees the c8-bishop. It keeps the main Open Sicilian set-ups available, but commits the d-pawn early and so lets White choose a different kind of game with Bb5+.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5, with a solid, flexible pawn structure. The cost is that the e6-pawn shuts in the c8-bishop for the time being. Against a slow White set-up Black can strike in the centre at once; against an Open Sicilian the game goes into a Kan or Taimanov structure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Qc7.strategy: Aims for a flexible, compact Sicilian set-up, as the queen eyes the c-file and e5. But it is committed before any piece, and Nb5 or Nd5 can hit it at once. Developing the knight first reaches the same structures without that exposure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and takes b5 from White's knight, a useful idea in many Sicilians. But it develops no piece, and White can build up without hurry.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which bears on e4 along the long diagonal. The move does little for d4 or e5 and commits Black to a slow set-up instead of a more active one.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Sets pawns on c5 and e5 against d4, as in an ordinary 1.e4 e5 game with the extra move ...c5. With both pawns advanced, neither can guard d5, so a white knight can settle there with Nd5. It gives up the usual Sicilian structure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and aims at a set-up with that bishop on the long diagonal. If White goes into an Open Sicilian, the knight on c3 keeps White from the Maróczy Bind with c4. It commits Black to the fianchetto before White has shown a plan.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it contests neither d4 nor e5 and needs another move to reach a useful square. White can also take it with Bxa6 bxa6, doubling Black's a-pawns but handing Black the bishop pair.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Qb6.strategy: Brings the queen out before any piece is developed, and it threatens nothing, because the c1-bishop guards b2. Nd5 or Na4 hits the queen at once, and White gains time while it retreats.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Qa5.strategy: Puts the queen on a5 while the pieces stay at home. It eyes c3, but the b- and d-pawns guard the knight, so the queen threatens nothing and White develops undisturbed.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Places the knight on the rim, where it eyes f5 and g4 but no central square. Once White plays d3 or d4, Bxh6 gxh6 doubles Black's pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 but runs into 3.e5, because the knight loses to Nxd5, Nxe4, Qxg4 or Qxh5 on every square except g8. Black must retreat, having spent two tempi while White gains space.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Takes b4 from White but does nothing for the centre or development. The a-pawn can no longer cover b5, so a white knight landing there cannot be driven away by ...a6.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Offers a pawn, because after 3.exd5 the queen cannot recapture: 3...Qxd5 loses it to Nxd5. Even if Black attacks the pawn with a developing move, White keeps it with natural development, and Black has little to show for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the king's knight and opens the diagonal from h5 to the king on e8. The pawn covers e5 but does nothing for development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: A rim-pawn move that does nothing for the centre or development, and gives White a free hand to build as it likes.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Advances the h-pawn without any developing or central purpose, and loosens g5 and the kingside. White continues to develop at leisure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Gives away a pawn: 3.Nxb5 or 3.Bxb5 takes it, and Black's quick development wins back a little time but not the pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Gives up a pawn: 3.exf5 takes it, and the c8-bishop cannot recapture past the d7-pawn. The opened diagonal from h5 to e8 also allows Qh5+ against Black's king.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Weakens the whole kingside and cannot hold the pawn: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 the queen attacks the rook on h8 and Bxg5 follows, with Black behind in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 c4.strategy: Gives away the pawn: 3.Bxc4 takes it at once and develops the bishop towards f7, while Black loses the c-pawn and with it all pressure on d4.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4.strategy: Stakes out kingside space and takes the e5 square from Black, aiming for a direct attack instead of a slow squeeze. The price is an early commitment of the f-pawn before the pieces are out and a looser king position; the game stays sharp, with White attacking the king and Black counterplaying on the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4.strategy: Gives up the closed set-up for open Sicilian play: White offers its d-pawn for Black's c-pawn to gain central space and open lines for the pieces. Played before the king's knight is out, it means the recapture on d4 is made by the queen, which Black can then hit with a developing move.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight and heads for the Open Sicilian by a different move order, with the knight already on c3. White gives up the quiet closed set-ups for the central break d4 and the main theory, where Black's early ...d6 is at home.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, the slow, solid way to play the Closed Sicilian. White keeps the pawn structure intact and the choice of plan open, at the cost of time: Black gets a free hand for queenside counterplay before White decides.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4.strategy: The natural exchange: Black trades the c-pawn for White's central d-pawn, as in every Sicilian. It opens the c-file for Black's rooks and leaves Black with a central pawn majority, while the d6 pawn keeps control of e5 and c5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on the e4 pawn, but allows White to exchange on c5 and trade queens: Black can only recapture with the king and loses the right to castle. Sound, but it hands White the easier game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks d4 without taking it, which leaves the tension in the centre unresolved. White can gain space with d5, driving the knight away from the centre and leaving Black a tempo behind.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: The natural recapture, and the only sound one: the pawn on d4 attacks the knight on c3 and no knight can take it yet. The queen stands in the centre at once, though Black gains time against it with a developing move, so White settles for a compact game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nb5.strategy: Sidesteps the attacked knight and eyes d6 and c7, but does not win the pawn back: ...e5 supports the pawn on d4, and White stays a pawn down with a knight that has lost time and can be harassed further.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops, but leaves the knight on c3 attacked by the pawn on d4: ...dxc3 wins a knight, and retaking the pawn on c3 gives White no compensation for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with tempo: the knight hits the queen on d4 and fights for the centre, so Black makes progress while White has to spend another move on the queen.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks the e4 pawn, which the knight on c3 already guards. Black keeps the b8-knight's tempo move against the queen in hand and stays flexible, at the price of letting White develop in peace for a move.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 e5.strategy: Drives the queen away at once and takes space, but leaves a hole on d5 that no Black pawn can control any more, and a backward d6 pawn. White's knight can settle on d5 and Black has to play carefully around it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Carlsen Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Steps the queen back to a square where it is not hit again at once, and clears d1 for long castling. White has lost time to Black's development, but keeps a sound, compact position and avoids the heavy theory of the Open Sicilian.

Pins the knight to the king along the diagonal, since d7 is empty, so the knight cannot take the queen. White is ready to give up the bishop for it and hopes that a lead in development makes up for handing Black the bishop pair.
Steps back along the file out of the knight's reach and keeps an eye on the centre. The queen blocks the king's bishop's natural diagonal, though, and Black goes on developing with gain of time.

Takes the queen all the way home: safe, but Black has developed a piece with tempo for free and the queen has done nothing since the pawn exchange. White keeps a sound position and gives up any hope of an advantage.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6.strategy: Answers the Grand Prix set-up in the most natural way: the knight develops and controls d4 and e5, challenging the e5 square that White's f-pawn stakes out. Black commits to nothing on the kingside yet and keeps the choice between a fianchetto and a counter-attack on the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto before committing the b8-knight, building a solid structure from the start. The bishop on g7 will press the long diagonal and the centre, while Black accepts that White holds more space on the kingside.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn at once with a developing move, so White has to react to it. White can answer by pushing the pawn to e5 with tempo against the knight, which takes space and makes the game sharper than Black may want.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3.strategy: Completes the kingside development and prepares castling, while the knight and the f-pawn together cover e5, and d4 stays available as a central break. The king's bishop remains free to choose its most active square, and White keeps the initiative on the kingside.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Bb5.strategy: Pins the knight to the king, since d7 is empty, and threatens to take on c6 and double Black's pawns. It costs time before the king's knight is out, and Black can break the pin with a developing move, so White's attack loses its edge.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7, the weak point of Black's camp, in the spirit of an attack on the king. The king's knight is still at home, so the pressure is not yet backed up, and the bishop can be chased from its post.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop to g7, where it presses the long diagonal and the centre. Black builds a solid pawn structure and counts on that bishop, and on queenside play, to answer White's kingside space.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, which the knight on c3 covers, and keeps both the fianchetto and a solid ...e6 set-up open. White can push e5 to chase the knight, which opens the game, so Black must be ready for sharper play.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Pins the knight against the queen and aims to trade it, but White can ask the bishop at once with h3 and gets the two bishops if Black takes on f3. Playable, yet it spends time for a small gain.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 g6 5.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once, with the f-pawn and knight already developed, instead of keeping the game closed. If Black takes, White's knight lands on a strong central square. The cost is that the early f4 has already loosened White's own king position, so the open game suits Black's counterplay as well.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 g6 5.Bb5.strategy: The positional choice: the bishop pins the knight to the king and threatens to take on c6, which would double Black's c-pawns. White develops quickly and plays for pressure on Black's structure rather than for an immediate attack.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 g6 5.Bc4.strategy: The more aggressive set-up: the bishop aims at f7 and, with the f-pawn and knight developed, supports a quick attack on the kingside. White plays for the king rather than for Black's structure, and the bishop stands more exposed.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 g6 5.d4.strategy: Takes the pawn, as Black does in every Sicilian: the c-pawn is traded for White's central pawn, the c-file opens, and White's recapture will put a piece on d4 that Black's pieces can then challenge.
Completes the fianchetto at once, but leaves the centre unresolved: White can take on c5 and trade queens, leaving Black with a passive knight on d8 or a king that has lost the right to castle.

Develops with an attack on e4, but leaves the tension in the centre unresolved. White can push e5 with tempo against the knight or take on c5, and Black has to sort out the centre before the kingside is developed.

The natural recapture: the knight takes a central post from which it eyes c6 and f5, and the d-file opens for the queen. White has more space and a lead in development, and plays for an attack against the king; Black's pieces will aim at the knight on d4.
Moves the attacked knight with a threat to retake on d4, but ...e5 supports the pawn on d4, so White does not win it back easily. White stays a pawn down with a knight that has gone offside.
Loses the queen: Black takes it with the knight and White's knight recaptures, so White has given the queen for a knight and a pawn.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop now presses on the knight on d4 along the long diagonal and takes its place for later castling. Black accepts less space for a solid position and a fight against White's central knight.

Develops with an attack on e4, which the knight on c3 guards, and keeps the bishop's fianchetto in reserve. White can strike with e5 to chase the knight, so Black has to meet the sharper play that follows.
Trades off White's best-placed knight: after the queen recaptures, ...Bg7 hits it at once, so Black gains time. The price is a developed piece, and White keeps the extra space in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.g3.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.g3.strategy: The slow, closed plan: the bishop will go to g2 to bear on the long diagonal and the centre, with the knight on c3 already covering d5. Against 2...e6 it allows ...d5 at once, since the e6 pawn supports that strike, which takes much of the sting out of White's set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4.strategy: The Grand Prix set-up: the f-pawn claims kingside space and the e5 square, preparing a direct attack on the king. Against 2...e6, though, Black has ...d5 ready at once, so White's plan has to prove itself against an immediate strike at the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nge2.strategy: Keeps White's options open: the f-pawn and the g-pawn both stay free, and d4 can still be played with a knight recapture. The knight on e2 is passive and blocks the king's bishop, and the set-up is not very challenging for Black.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nf3.strategy: The most flexible reply: the knight develops and covers d4, so White can open the game in the manner of a regular Sicilian with a central pawn break whenever it suits, or keep it closed. Against the immediate ...d5 the centre opens into an even game with natural development for both.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight and eyes d4 and e5, keeping ...d5 ready, which the e6 pawn already supports. Black spends no time on a kingside commitment, because the strike in the centre is the answer to White's attacking set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre before White's attack has started: the e6 pawn supports the push and the e4 pawn is defended only by the knight. White must clarify the centre at once, either by exchanging, which opens the e-file for an even game, or by pushing past the pawn, which gives a closed structure where the f-pawn is already committed.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 d6.strategy: Builds a compact pawn wall that keeps any e5 push from White in check and prepares quiet development. It gives up the central strike for the time being and leaves the light-squared bishop only the d7 square, so Black accepts a cramped but solid game while White gets on with the kingside plan.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and brings castling closer, while it covers e5 and d4 beside the f-pawn. It leaves the centre open to Black's strike, and White accepts that, counting on the pieces to be better placed for an attack.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight at once, but with the d7 pawn still in place there is no pin, and Black replies by putting the knight on d4, where it hits the bishop and holds a strong central square. White has spent time with one piece and must trade it or retreat.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.g3.strategy: Combines the f-pawn's space with a fianchetto, aiming at a slow, solid squeeze of the centre from the long diagonal instead of a direct attack. It is sound, but Black can strike at e4 immediately, before the bishop has reached its post, and the plan loses much of its bite.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 d5.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 d5.strategy: The thematic strike that the e6 set-up prepares: Black challenges the e4 pawn at once and claims a share of the centre while White's attack is still on paper. White's pieces have to react to the pressure on e4 before the kingside plan can start.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 Nge7.strategy: Develops the knight to a square where an e5 push gains no tempo and where it supports the d5 break, which stays available. The price is a knight that blocks the dark-squared bishop for now, so Black accepts a slower development in exchange for a sturdy position.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 d6.strategy: Guards e5 with a pawn and keeps a compact centre, but it gives up the thematic ...d5 strike and leaves the light-squared bishop only the d7 square. White can develop and castle at leisure, so Black faces a passive game with little counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 d5 5.Bb5.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 d5 5.Bb5.strategy: Pins the knight on c6 to the king along the b5-e8 diagonal, so the tension in the centre now has a second front. Bxc6+ would double Black's pawns, and Black has to settle the centre and the pin at the same time.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 d5 5.exd.strategy: Settles the tension by taking: after the recapture with the e-pawn the e-file opens and the centre is nearly symmetrical, with the f-pawn keeping Black's pieces off e5. White develops freely and castles, and the attacking plan on the kingside gives way to an even game in which the better-coordinated pieces decide.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.f4 Nc6 4.Nf3 d5 5.e5.strategy: Closes the centre and takes space, much as in an advanced French structure. The pawn needs constant support from the f-pawn and the knight, however, and Black can undermine it with a pawn break, while White's kingside pawns are tied to its defence.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.g3 d5.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Korchnoi Defence
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre before White's bishop has reached g2 and so spoils the closed plan: the e6 pawn supports the push. White's e4 pawn is attacked at once and defended only by the knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight to the centre and covers d4 and e5 before the d-pawn is committed. Black mirrors White's closed set-up and keeps ...d5 for the right moment, heading for a manoeuvring game in which the pieces are well placed against the fianchetto.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.g3 d6.strategy: A solid, patient move that defends the c5 pawn and covers e5. It passes up the chance to strike in the centre before the fianchetto is complete, though, so White gets the slow, closed game it was aiming for and Black has to find play on the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nge2 a6.strategy: A flexible waiting move that takes b5 from White's pieces and prepares the queenside expansion ...b5. Black keeps every set-up open, including the knight's best square, and spends a tempo on a useful move against a White set-up that is not very threatening.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nge2 Nc6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight eyes d4, so if White opens the centre Black recaptures with a comfortable open Sicilian, and if White closes it with a fianchetto Black has a sound closed game. Black leaves the pawn moves for later, and the passive knight on e2 gives White's set-up little bite.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nge2 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once: the e6 pawn supports the push, and the knight on e2 does not help White fight for d5. Black gets central space and a free game before White's flexible plan has taken shape, and an exchange on d5 leaves a healthy, even position.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nge2 a6 4.g3.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nge2 a6 4.g3.strategy: Chooses the closed route: the pawn frees the king's bishop, which was blocked by the knight on e2, for the fianchetto on g2. White still keeps d4 in hand to open the game later with a knight recapture, which is the point of the flexible set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nge2 a6 4.d4.strategy: The reason for the set-up: White opens the game and, after the capture, recaptures with the knight into a regular open Sicilian with the knight already well placed on d4. White commits to a sharp, open fight where the extra waiting move ...a6 is of use to Black, but White has avoided every closed-game concession.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Nge2 a6 4.d3.strategy: A modest, flexible move that supports e4 and frees the dark-squared bishop, keeping both a fianchetto and a kingside advance possible. It is sound but slow, and Black's queenside expansion with the extra ...a6 tempo gains more space than White's set-up creates in return.
